vignette:
# Margaret

Margaret sits in the studio she built with her husband thirty years ago, surrounded by the half-finished pieces that have accumulated over the past two years. She runs her hand along a bronze torso she abandoned last spring, feeling the cool metal beneath her fingertips. At sixty-three, she has spent most of her adult life working with her hands, translating the human form into something timeless. Now, the work feels impossible.

The assault happened on a February evening four years ago. She had stayed late at the community arts center where she taught sculpture classes twice a week, working on a commission in the studio after everyone had left. A man she didn't recognize forced his way in through the back entrance. What followed was violent and brief, though Margaret experiences it as both simultaneously. The details arrive in fragments—the smell of stale coffee on his breath, the cold concrete floor pressing against her hip, the way her hands, which had been holding a clay modeling tool, went numb.

She reported it to the police. There was an investigation. Nothing came of it. The man was never found. For the first year, Margaret told herself she was managing. She returned to teaching. She created a series of small bronze heads that critics called her most emotionally raw work. Her husband, David, was careful with her, which somehow made everything worse.

By year two, the texture of the trauma had changed. Margaret found herself unable to be alone in the studio. The space that had always felt sacred now felt dangerous. She'd arrive with intention, stand among her tools and materials, and feel her chest tighten. Her breath would become shallow. Sometimes she would leave without touching anything. Other times, she'd force herself to work, gripping the clay with an intensity that bordered on violence, only to find herself sobbing without understanding why.

Now, in year four, Margaret exists in a state of hypervigilance that exhausts her. She cannot hear a car door slam without her body flooding with adrenaline. She locks the studio door obsessively—checking it five, six, sometimes ten times before she can settle. When David approaches her from behind, even to kiss her neck, she flinches violently. They have stopped being intimate. He has stopped trying.

Sleep is fragmented. She wakes at three or four in the morning, her heart racing, sometimes with no memory of what she was dreaming. Other nights, the dreams are vivid and relentless—she is always back on that floor, always unable to move or call for help, always aware of the danger arriving from behind her.

The teaching stopped eighteen months ago. She couldn't manage the vulnerability of being around students, couldn't bear the questions about why she wasn't creating anymore. David suggested she take a break. The break has become something else entirely.

What troubles Margaret most is not the fear, though the fear is constant and consuming. It is the loss of herself. She was a sculptor. That identity was not separate from her—it was woven through her being as fundamentally as her breath. Now, when she looks at her hands, she sees them as they were that night: powerless. The studio, once a place of creation and solace, has become a monument to what was taken from her. She sits among her tools and her unfinished work, waiting for something to shift, waiting to feel like herself again, and the waiting itself has become another kind of unbearable.
